memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, their offering is to be of the finest flour. They are to pour olive oil on it, put incense on it.'" - Lev 2:1 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
After a chapter soaked in blood, this is a surprise. Here is an offering with no animal, no knife, no death. Just flour, oil, and incense.

The grain offering (Hebrew minchah, meaning a gift or tribute) was not primarily about sin. It was about acknowledging that everything a person had came from God. Flour meant harvest. Harvest meant rain, soil, seasons, strength to work — every one of them God's doing. Bringing flour was a way of saying: I know where this came from.

Notice the word finest. The Israelite could not scoop up coarse leftovers from the bottom of the sack. Fine flour took extra grinding, extra sifting, extra effort. Worship cost time before it cost anything else.

There is something here for people who feel they have nothing dramatic to offer God. Not every act of worship involves crisis or sacrifice of the heroic kind. Sometimes worship is simply bringing God the ordinary produce of your ordinary week — your work, your wages, your cooking, your studies — and saying, this came from You, and I return it to You.

Whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31). The kitchen and the office can be an altar.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I recognise God as the source of my daily provision, or do I quietly credit myself?
2. What ordinary part of my week could I consciously offer to God this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, everything I hold came first from Your hand. Teach me to bring back to You the ordinary fruit of my days, and to bring it carefully. Amen.
